title: Essential Swedish Grammar
subtitle: A1 → B2 Grammar Companion to 'Essential Swedish: 650 Words & Phrases'
howToUse: Work through one chapter at a time. Read the summary, study the rules and say every example out loud using the pronunciation guide, then try the practice items before checking the answers. Each chapter has a 'key_takeaway' you can use as a flashcard.
pronunciationGuide: Every example has a 'pron' field written with English spelling patterns so you can sound it out without IPA. It is an approximation: Swedish pitch accent and vowel length can't be shown fully. Refine with native audio. Capital letters (e.g. 'tickehr OMM') mark the stressed particle in particle verbs. Key: ah = father · eh = bed · ee = see · oo = boot · oh = for · ai = air · ur = fur (covers ö) · ew = Swedish u / y (rounded 'ee') · ch = the soft k sound in kött, känna · sh = the sj / skj / stj sound · y = both consonant j and soft g (as in gilla, göra)

parts.title: Part 1: Nouns
parts.subtitle: Gender, definite forms, plurals and how Swedish puts 'the' on the end of the word.

chapters.title: Noun Gender: en-words and ett-words
chapters.summary: Every Swedish noun is either an en-word (common gender, about 75% of nouns) or an ett-word (neuter, about 25%). The gender decides the article, the definite ending, adjective endings and possessive forms, so always learn a noun together with en or ett.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Learn every noun as 'en bil', 'ett hus' — never just 'bil' or 'hus'.

rules.title: The indefinite article: en / ett ('a/an')
rules.explanation: Use 'en' before en-words and 'ett' before ett-words. There is no reliable rule for every word, so gender must be memorised, but the hints below cover a lot of ground.

rules.title: Helpful gender patterns
rules.explanation: Most words for people and animals are en-words (but note ett barn, ett djur). Certain endings strongly predict gender.

examples.note: Exception: a person, but an ett-word.

rows: en man, en kvinna, en hund (exceptions: ett barn, ett djur)

rules.title: Why gender matters
rules.explanation: Gender changes almost every word around the noun: the definite ending (bilen / huset), adjectives (en stor bil / ett stort hus), and possessives (min bil / mitt hus).

commonMistakes.why: hus is an ett-word.
bil is an en-word.

chapters.title: The Definite Form: 'the' as an Ending
chapters.summary: Swedish has no separate word for 'the' before a single noun. Instead an ending is added: -en/-n for en-words and -et/-t for ett-words.
chapters.keyTakeaway: bil → bilen (the car), hus → huset (the house).

rules.title: en-words take -en (or -n after a vowel)
rules.explanation: Add -en to en-words ending in a consonant. If the word already ends in a vowel, add only -n.

examples.english: The girl is reading the book.

rules.title: ett-words take -et (or -t after a vowel)
rules.explanation: Add -et to ett-words ending in a consonant, and -t if they end in a vowel.

examples.english: The apple is on the table.

rules.title: Words ending in unstressed -el, -er, -en
rules.explanation: These usually add only -n or -t, and some ett-words drop the e of the last syllable.

commonMistakes.why: With no adjective, 'the' is only the ending — no separate den/det.
Words ending in a vowel add only -t / -n.

practice.explanation: Short vowel + m doubles the consonant: rum → rummet.

chapters.title: Plural Nouns: The Five Groups
chapters.summary: Swedish plurals use five main endings: -or, -ar, -er, -n and no ending. The noun's gender and how it ends usually tell you which group it belongs to.
chapters.keyTakeaway: -a words → -or; most short en-words → -ar; loanwords → -er; ett-words ending in a vowel → -n; ett-words ending in a consonant → no change.

rules.title: The five plural groups
rules.explanation: Use this table as your main reference. Group 2 is the largest group for en-words, and group 5 is the most common for ett-words.

rows: most one-syllable en-words; en-words ending in -e, -ing, -el, -er
en bil / en pojke / en tidning
loanwords, words with stress on the last syllable, some with vowel change
en station / en park / en hand
ett-words ending in a consonant; en-words ending in -are, -er (people)

rules.title: Dropping the last -e or -el/-er vowel
rules.explanation: En-words ending in -e drop the -e before -ar. Words ending in -el, -er, -en usually lose the e.

rules.title: Irregular plurals with a vowel change
rules.explanation: A small group of common words change their vowel (like English man → men). Learn these as vocabulary.

commonMistakes.why: ett-words ending in a consonant don't change in the plural.
En-words ending in -are have no plural ending.
bok is irregular.

chapters.title: The Definite Plural ('the cars', 'the houses')
chapters.summary: To say 'the' in the plural, add -na to plurals ending in -or/-ar/-er, -a to plurals ending in -n, and -en to plurals with no ending.
chapters.keyTakeaway: bilar → bilarna, äpplen → äpplena, hus → husen.

rules.title: The four forms of a noun
rules.explanation: Every noun has four forms. Learning all four for a new word is the fastest way to master Swedish nouns.

commonMistakes.why: Plurals with no ending take -en.
-are words drop the final -e: lärare → lärarna.

practice.prompt: The books are on the table.

chapters.title: Double Definiteness: den stora bilen
chapters.summary: When an adjective stands before a definite noun, Swedish marks 'the' twice: once with den/det/de in front, and once with the noun ending.
chapters.keyTakeaway: the big car = den stora bilen (den + adjective-a + noun-en).

rules.title: den / det / de + adjective + definite noun
rules.explanation: Use den for en-words, det for ett-words and de for all plurals. The adjective takes -a (see 3.2), and the noun keeps its definite ending.

rules.title: No double definiteness after possessives or genitives
rules.explanation: After min, din, hans, Annas etc., the adjective still takes -a, but the noun stays indefinite and there is no den/det/de.

rules.title: Formal 'denna/detta/dessa' takes an indefinite noun
rules.explanation: In formal writing, denna/detta/dessa ('this/these') is followed by an indefinite noun. In speech, 'den här bilen' is far more common (see 2.4).

commonMistakes.why: The noun needs its definite ending too.
Possessives already make the noun definite.

chapters.title: Possession with -s (Genitive)
chapters.summary: Add -s directly to a name or noun to show ownership — no apostrophe. The thing owned stays in the indefinite form.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Annas bil (Anna's car) — no apostrophe, and the noun after it has no definite ending.

rules.title: Add -s, no apostrophe
rules.explanation: The -s can attach to names, indefinite nouns, definite nouns and plurals.

rules.title: Names ending in -s, -x, -z
rules.explanation: Add nothing, or use an apostrophe in writing.

commonMistakes.why: Swedish doesn't use an apostrophe before the -s.
After a genitive the noun stays indefinite.

chapters.title: Compound Nouns
chapters.summary: Swedish builds new nouns by joining words into one. The LAST part decides the gender and the plural.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Write compounds as one word: kaffekopp, not 'kaffe kopp'.

rules.title: The last word decides everything
rules.explanation: en kaffekopp is an en-word because kopp is; ett sovrum is an ett-word because rum is.

rules.title: Linking letters: -s- and dropped vowels
rules.explanation: Often a linking -s- is added, especially after words ending in -ning, -het, -tion or -dom, or the first word drops a final -a/-e.

rules.title: Never split a compound
rules.explanation: Writing compounds as two words (särskrivning) can change the meaning completely and is one of the most noticed errors in Swedish.

examples.note: Split as 'sjuk sköterska' it means 'a sick nurse'.

commonMistakes.why: One word, and the gender comes from 'kopp'.

parts.title: Part 2: Pronouns
parts.subtitle: Subject and object forms, the tricky sin/sitt/sina, reflexives, 'this/that', det and man, and words like någon and ingen.

chapters.title: Personal Pronouns: Subject and Object
chapters.summary: Like English I/me and he/him, Swedish pronouns have a subject form (who does the action) and an object form (who receives it or follows a preposition).
chapters.keyTakeaway: jag → mig, du → dig, han → honom, hon → henne, vi → oss, ni → er, de → dem.

rules.title: The full pronoun table
rules.explanation: mig, dig and sig are pronounced 'may', 'day', 'say' (often spelled mej, dej, sej informally). De and dem are both pronounced 'dom' in everyday speech.

rules.title: Object form after prepositions
rules.explanation: After a preposition (med, till, för, på, om...) always use the object form.

rules.title: 'den' vs 'det' for 'it'
rules.explanation: Use den when 'it' refers to an en-word and det when it refers to an ett-word. Use det for general statements and situations.

examples.swedish: Var är boken? Den ligger på bordet.
examples.english: Where is the book? It's on the table.
examples.pronunciation: vahr air boochehn? dehn liggehr poh boordeht.

examples.swedish: Var är huset? Det ligger där.
examples.english: Where's the house? It's over there.
examples.pronunciation: vahr air hewseht? deh liggehr dair.

commonMistakes.why: 'you' is the object here, so use dig.
Subject is de; dem is only the object form, even though both sound like 'dom'.

chapters.title: Reflexive Possessives: sin / sitt / sina
chapters.summary: Swedish distinguishes between 'his own' and 'someone else's'. When the owner is the third-person subject (han, hon, den, det, de, a name) of the same clause, use sin/sitt/sina instead of hans/hennes/deras.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Erik tar sin bil = Erik takes his (own) car. Erik tar hans bil = Erik takes his (another man's) car.

rules.title: Forms: sin (en), sitt (ett), sina (plural)
rules.explanation: sin/sitt/sina agree with the thing owned, just like min/mitt/mina.

examples.english: The children play with their (own) friends.

rules.title: sin vs hans: the meaning changes
rules.explanation: Using hans/hennes/deras when the subject owns the thing implies it belongs to someone else.

rules.title: Never use sin to describe the subject itself
rules.explanation: sin points BACK to the subject, so it can never be part of the subject. Also, it is not used with jag, du, vi, ni — those keep min, din, vår, er.

commonMistakes.why: sin can't be in the subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: Hon tvättar hennes bil. (meaning her own)
commonMistakes.why: The subject is the owner, so use sin.

practice.prompt: Pelle målar ___ rum. (his own, 'rum' is ett)

chapters.title: Reflexive Pronouns: mig, dig, sig...
chapters.summary: A reflexive pronoun is used when the subject and the object are the same person ('I wash myself'). Swedish uses the normal object forms, except for the third person, which uses sig.
chapters.keyTakeaway: jag … mig, du … dig, han/hon/de … sig, vi … oss, ni … er.

rules.title: The reflexive forms
rules.explanation: Swedish uses reflexives much more than English. Many verbs always need one (see 4.8).

rules.title: sig själv for emphasis
rules.explanation: Add själv / själva ('self/selves') to stress that it's really the same person.

commonMistakes.why: 'henne' would mean another woman.

chapters.title: This and That: den här, det där...
chapters.summary: To say 'this' and 'that', Swedish combines den/det/de with här (here) or där (there). The noun takes the definite ending.
chapters.keyTakeaway: den här bilen (this car), det där huset (that house), de här skorna (these shoes).

rules.title: The pattern
rules.explanation: Pick den/det/de by gender and number, add här (this/these) or där (that/those), then the noun in definite form.

examples.swedish: Vem bor i det där huset?
examples.pronunciation: vemm boor ee deh dair hewseht?

examples.swedish: De här skorna är för små.
examples.pronunciation: dom hair skoornah air furr smoh.

rules.title: Det här är... (this is...)
rules.explanation: When pointing something out or introducing someone, always use 'det här' / 'det där', no matter what gender the noun is.

rules.title: Formal: denna / detta / dessa
rules.explanation: Common in writing. These take an indefinite noun.

commonMistakes.why: The noun needs the definite ending after den här.
Use det här when presenting someone or something.

chapters.title: det as a Dummy Subject, det finns, and man
chapters.summary: A Swedish main clause always needs a subject. When there is no real one ('it's raining'), use det. 'There is/are' is det finns, and 'one/you/people' in general is man.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Det regnar. Det finns en bank här. Man säger så.

rules.title: det for weather, time and situations
rules.explanation: Use det wherever English uses 'it' without a real subject.

rules.title: det finns = there is / there are
rules.explanation: det finns means something exists. det är is used for 'it is'. Compare: Det finns kaffe (there is coffee) / Det är kaffe (it is coffee).

examples.swedish: Det står en man vid dörren.
examples.english: There's a man standing by the door.
examples.pronunciation: deh stohr ehn mahn veed durrehn.

rules.title: man = one / you / people (in general)
rules.explanation: man is very common in Swedish and often replaces the passive. The object form is en and the possessive is ens.

examples.english: That's what you say in Swedish.
You're not allowed to smoke here.

commonMistakes.why: A subject is required.
For existence, use det finns.

practice.prompt: Is there a pharmacy near here?
practice.answer: Finns det ett apotek här i närheten?
acceptedAnswers: Finns det ett apotek här i närheten?

practice.prompt: You (people in general) eat a lot of fish in Sweden.
practice.answer: Man äter mycket fisk i Sverige.
acceptedAnswers: Man äter mycket fisk i Sverige.

chapters.title: Indefinite Pronouns: någon, ingen, all, varje...
chapters.summary: Words like 'some', 'no', 'all' and 'every' change form to match en-words, ett-words and plurals.
chapters.keyTakeaway: någon/något/några, ingen/inget/inga, all/allt/alla — en / ett / plural.

rules.title: The forms
rules.explanation: Choose the form by what the word refers to.

rules.title: ingen vs inte någon (B1)
rules.explanation: ingen/inget/inga can only be used when it would stand directly after the finite verb in a simple tense. With auxiliaries (har, ska, kan...) or in subordinate clauses, use inte någon/något/några instead.

examples.swedish: Han sa att han inte hade några pengar.
examples.english: He said he didn't have any money.
examples.pronunciation: hahn sah att hahn eenteh hahdeh nohgrah pehngahr.

commonMistakes.why: With har + supine, use inte någon.
äpple is an ett-word.

parts.title: Part 3: Adjectives & Adverbs
parts.subtitle: How adjectives change with gender and definiteness, comparing things, and turning adjectives into adverbs.

chapters.title: Adjective Agreement: stor, stort, stora
chapters.summary: In the indefinite form, adjectives have three forms: the base form for en-words, +t for ett-words, and +a for plurals. This applies both before the noun and after 'är'.
chapters.keyTakeaway: en stor bil, ett stort hus, stora bilar/hus. Bilen är stor, huset är stort, husen är stora.

rules.title: The basic pattern
rules.explanation: The adjective agrees with the noun it describes, whether it stands before the noun or after a verb like är or blir.

rules.title: Spelling changes in the -t form
rules.explanation: Long vowel + d becomes -tt; a stressed final vowel gets -tt; adjectives already ending in consonant + t don't change; -ig just adds -t.

rules.title: Irregular and unchanging adjectives
rules.explanation: liten is fully irregular. Some adjectives never change: bra, extra, gratis, rosa, lila, and many ending in -a or -e.

commonMistakes.why: hus is an ett-word, so the adjective takes -t even after är.
d + t becomes tt.
The plural of liten is små.

chapters.title: The Definite Form of Adjectives
chapters.summary: When the noun is definite — after den/det/de, a possessive (min, hans), a genitive (Annas) or den här — the adjective ends in -a in every gender and number.
chapters.keyTakeaway: den stora bilen, det stora huset, min stora bil, Annas stora hus — always -a.

rules.title: Always -a after definite words
rules.explanation: Words that trigger the definite adjective: den/det/de, den här/där, min/din/hans/sin etc., genitives, and denna/detta/dessa.

rules.title: liten → lilla, and the optional -e
rules.explanation: liten becomes lilla in the definite singular (and små in the plural). In formal or older Swedish, an adjective describing a male person may end in -e: den gamle mannen. The -a form is always correct.

commonMistakes.why: After a possessive, the adjective takes -a.
Definite form of liten is lilla.

chapters.title: Comparison: varmare, varmast
chapters.summary: Most adjectives add -are (more) and -ast (most). A group of short, common adjectives changes vowel and adds -re / -st. Long adjectives use mer and mest.
chapters.keyTakeaway: varm → varmare → varmast; stor → större → störst; bra → bättre → bäst.

rules.title: Regular: -are / -ast
rules.explanation: This is the default pattern.

examples.swedish: Det är varmare i dag än i går.
examples.pronunciation: deh air vahrmahreh ee dah ehn ee gohr.

rules.title: Vowel change + -re / -st
rules.explanation: A handful of very common adjectives. Learn them as a set.

examples.swedish: Min bror är yngre än jag.
examples.english: My brother is younger than me.
examples.pronunciation: meen broor air ewngreh ehn yah.

rules.title: Irregular
rules.explanation: These are fully irregular and very frequent.

examples.english: She's the oldest in the family.

rules.title: mer / mest for long adjectives
rules.explanation: Use mer and mest with long adjectives, words ending in -isk, and participles.

examples.swedish: Boken är mer intressant än filmen.
examples.english: The book is more interesting than the film.
examples.pronunciation: boochehn air mehr intrehsahnt ehn feelmehn.

rules.title: än (than) and lika ... som (as ... as)
rules.explanation: After än, both jag and mig are heard; jag is the more formal choice.

examples.swedish: Hon är lika lång som jag.
examples.english: She is as tall as me.
examples.pronunciation: hoon air leekah lohng soom yah.

examples.english: The train is faster than the bus.

commonMistakes.why: bra is irregular.
Short adjectives use endings, not mer.
'than' is än; 'som' is used in lika ... som.

practice.prompt: Det här kaffet är ___ än det andra. (god)

chapters.title: Superlatives Before Nouns: den största
chapters.summary: Before a noun, superlatives take the definite form: -ast becomes -aste, and -st becomes -sta. They follow the double-definite pattern.
chapters.keyTakeaway: den billigaste bilen, det största huset, de bästa vännerna.

rules.title: Attributive superlative endings
rules.explanation: Add -e to -ast, and -a to -st.

examples.swedish: Det är den bästa filmen jag har sett.
examples.english: It's the best film I've seen.
examples.pronunciation: deh air dehn bestah feelmehn yah hahr sehtt.

rules.title: Useful fixed phrases
rules.explanation: Common expressions with superlatives.

commonMistakes.why: Before a noun, -ast becomes -aste.

chapters.title: Adverbs from Adjectives
chapters.summary: To describe HOW something is done, use the -t form of the adjective (the same as the ett-form).
chapters.keyTakeaway: snabb → snabbt: Han kör snabbt (He drives fast).

rules.title: Use the ett-form as an adverb
rules.explanation: This is the Swedish equivalent of English '-ly'. Adjectives that never change (bra) stay the same.

rules.title: Intensifiers: mycket, ganska, för, så
rules.explanation: These go before adjectives and adverbs: mycket (very), ganska (quite), för (too), så (so), väldigt (really), lite (a bit).

commonMistakes.why: Describing how she talks needs the adverb (-t).

parts.title: Part 4: Verbs
parts.subtitle: Tenses, the four verb groups, irregular verbs, modals, reflexive and particle verbs, the passive and more. Good news: Swedish verbs never change for person — jag, du, han, vi, de all use the same form.

chapters.title: Infinitive & Present Tense: The Four Verb Groups
chapters.summary: Swedish verbs fall into four groups. The present tense ends in -r, and it is the same for every person. The present also covers English 'I am doing' and often the near future.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Group 1: prata → pratar. Group 2: köpa → köper. Group 3: bo → bor. Group 4 (irregular): skriva → skriver, gå → går.

rules.title: One form for all persons
rules.explanation: Unlike English (I speak / she speaks), Swedish uses one present form for everyone.

rules.title: The four groups
rules.explanation: The infinitive usually ends in -a. Short verbs (group 3) end in another vowel.

rows: mostly -er or -r; past tense changes vowel

rules.title: Irregular present forms to memorise
rules.explanation: These very common verbs don't follow the pattern.

rules.title: Present tense for the future
rules.explanation: With a time word, the present often describes the future.

examples.swedish: Jag åker till Göteborg i morgon.
examples.pronunciation: yah ohkehr till yurtehbory ee morron.

commonMistakes.why: No extra ending for he/she.
Swedish has no 'am + -ing' form; the present tense covers it.

chapters.title: The Imperative (Commands)
chapters.summary: The imperative is the verb's stem — the infinitive minus the final -a for groups 2 and 4. Group 1 and 3 verbs look like the infinitive.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Prata! Köp! Bo! Skriv! — and soften it with 'är du snäll' or by asking 'Kan du...?'

rules.title: How to form it
rules.explanation: Group 1 keeps the -a; group 2 and 4 drop it; group 3 stays the same.

rules.title: Making it polite
rules.explanation: Swedish rarely uses 'please' (snälla). Politeness comes from questions or softening phrases.

rules.title: Negative commands
rules.explanation: Put inte after the verb.

commonMistakes.why: inte comes after the verb.

chapters.title: The Past Tense (Preteritum)
chapters.summary: The simple past ('I talked', 'I bought') depends on the verb group: -ade, -de/-te, -dde, or a vowel change for strong verbs.
chapters.keyTakeaway: pratade, ringde, köpte, bodde, skrev.

rules.title: Weak verbs (groups 1–3)
rules.explanation: Group 2 splits: -te if the stem ends in a voiceless consonant (k, p, s, t, x), otherwise -de.

examples.english: We talked for a long time.

rows: stem (k, p, s, t, x) + te

rules.title: Strong verbs (group 4): vowel change
rules.explanation: No ending — the vowel changes. See chapter 4.7 for the full table.

rules.title: When to use the past tense
rules.explanation: Use preteritum for finished actions at a specific time in the past (i går, förra veckan, 2019, när jag var liten).

examples.swedish: Förra sommaren reste vi till Italien.
examples.english: Last summer we travelled to Italy.
examples.pronunciation: furrah sommahrehn rehsteh vee till itahliehn.

commonMistakes.why: p is voiceless, so -te.
gå is irregular.

chapters.title: Perfect & Pluperfect: har/hade + Supine
chapters.summary: The perfect ('I have done') is har + supine; the pluperfect ('I had done') is hade + supine. The supine is a special verb form used only after ha.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag har pratat / köpt / bott / skrivit. Jag hade redan ätit.

rules.title: Forming the supine
rules.explanation: Each group has its own supine ending.

examples.swedish: Jag har bott här i två år.
examples.english: I've lived here for two years.
examples.pronunciation: yah hahr bott hair ee tvoh ohr.

examples.swedish: Hon har aldrig varit i Sverige.
examples.english: She has never been to Sweden.
examples.pronunciation: hoon hahr ahldree vahreet ee svehryeh.

rules.title: Perfect vs past tense
rules.explanation: Use the perfect when the time is unspecified or the result still matters now. As soon as you name a finished time (i går, 2020, förra året), use the past tense.

rules.title: Pluperfect: hade + supine
rules.explanation: For something that happened before another past event.

examples.swedish: Tåget hade redan gått när vi kom.
examples.english: The train had already left when we arrived.
examples.pronunciation: tohgeht hahdeh rehdahn gott nair vee komm.

rules.title: Dropping har/hade in subordinate clauses (B2)
rules.explanation: In written Swedish, har/hade is often left out in subordinate clauses.

examples.english: I know that she has quit.

commonMistakes.wrong: Jag har sett filmen i går.
commonMistakes.why: A specific past time needs the past tense.
Strong verbs take -it.

chapters.title: Talking About the Future
chapters.summary: Swedish has three main ways to talk about the future: ska (plans and intentions), kommer att (predictions), and the plain present with a time word.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag ska börja en kurs (plan). Det kommer att regna (prediction). Vi ses i morgon (present + time).

rules.title: ska + infinitive: plans, decisions, promises
rules.explanation: Use ska when someone has decided or intends to do something.

examples.english: I'm going to start a Swedish course.

examples.swedish: Vad ska du göra i helgen?
examples.english: What are you doing this weekend?
examples.pronunciation: vahd skah dew yurrah ee helyehn?

rules.title: kommer att + infinitive: predictions
rules.explanation: Use kommer att for things no one decides — weather, results, consequences. In speech the att is often dropped.

examples.swedish: Det kommer att regna i morgon.
examples.pronunciation: deh kommehr att rehgnah ee morron.

rules.title: Present + time expression
rules.explanation: Very common for scheduled or near-future events.

commonMistakes.right: Det kommer att regna i morgon.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: deh kommehr att rehgnah ee morron.
commonMistakes.why: No one decides the weather — use kommer att. ('Det ska regna' means 'it's supposed to rain', a forecast.)

practice.prompt: Jag ___ ringa mamma i kväll. (I've decided)
We're going to buy a house.

chapters.title: Modal Verbs: kan, vill, ska, måste, får, bör
chapters.summary: Modal verbs are followed directly by an infinitive — never with att. Watch out for 'får inte' (must not) vs 'behöver inte' (don't have to).
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag kan simma (not 'kan att simma'). Du får inte röka = you must not smoke.

rules.title: The modals and their forms
rules.explanation: All modals are followed by a bare infinitive.

rows: may, be allowed to; get to

rules.title: får inte vs behöver inte
rules.explanation: får inte = not allowed / must not. behöver inte = don't need to. 'måste inte' is heard but is ambiguous — avoid it.

rules.title: brukar = usually (habit)
rules.explanation: brukar works like a modal (no att) and is the natural way to talk about habits.

examples.swedish: Jag brukar dricka te på kvällen.
examples.english: I usually drink tea in the evening.
examples.pronunciation: yah brewkahr drickah teh poh kvellehn.

rules.title: Modal without a main verb
rules.explanation: With a direction word, the movement verb is often dropped.

examples.english: I have to go home now.

commonMistakes.why: No att after modals.

commonMistakes.wrong: Du måste inte röka här. (meaning 'not allowed')
commonMistakes.why: Prohibition is får inte.

chapters.title: Strong & Irregular Verbs: The Essential Table
chapters.summary: About 100 common verbs are strong or irregular. They change vowel in the past tense and usually take -it in the supine. These are the ones you'll use daily.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Learn them in four forms: dricka – dricker – drack – druckit.

rules.title: Patterns that help
rules.explanation: Many strong verbs follow vowel patterns. Spotting the pattern makes new verbs easier.

examples.swedish: Hon har sjungit i kör i tio år.
examples.english: She has sung in a choir for ten years.
examples.pronunciation: hoon hahr shungeet ee chur ee teeoo ohr.

rules.title: The essential irregular verb table
rules.explanation: Infinitive – present – past – supine.

examples.english: He took the bus to work.

commonMistakes.why: äta is strong.
Strong verbs take -it in the supine.

chapters.title: Reflexive Verbs
chapters.summary: Many Swedish verbs need a reflexive pronoun (mig, dig, sig, oss, er) even when English doesn't use 'myself'. Learn them with 'sig': sätta sig, känna sig.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag sätter mig. Hon känner sig trött. Vi har bestämt oss.

rules.title: Common reflexive verbs
rules.explanation: The pronoun changes with the subject (see 2.3).

examples.english: Hurry, the bus is leaving soon!

rules.title: Word order with reflexives
rules.explanation: In inverted sentences the reflexive follows the subject; inte comes after the reflexive in simple tenses.

examples.swedish: I dag känner jag mig bättre.
examples.pronunciation: ee dah chennehr yah may bettreh.

commonMistakes.why: lära (without mig) means 'to teach'.
känna sig = feel (a state).

practice.prompt: I go to bed at eleven.

chapters.title: Particle Verbs
chapters.summary: A particle verb is a verb + a small stressed word (om, på, upp, ut, av, ihåg...) that together create a new meaning — like English 'give up' or 'turn off'. The particle carries the stress.
chapters.keyTakeaway: tycka om = like, hälsa på = visit, komma ihåg = remember, se ut = look (appear).

rules.title: Essential particle verbs
rules.explanation: Stress the particle when speaking: 'tycka OM', 'hälsa PÅ'. Without stress, 'hälsa på' means 'say hello to'.

examples.swedish: Vi hälsar på mormor i helgen.
examples.pronunciation: vee helsahr POH moormoor ee helyehn.

rules.title: Word order: the particle stays after the verb
rules.explanation: Unlike English 'turn it off', the particle normally comes before an object pronoun. Adjectives and objects with se ut go between verb and particle.

rules.title: Particle moves to the front in participles (B2)
rules.explanation: When a particle verb becomes a participle or noun, the particle is usually attached at the front.

commonMistakes.why: The particle comes before the object.
inte goes after the finite verb, before the particle.

chapters.title: The Passive: s-passive and bli-passive
chapters.summary: The passive puts the focus on what happens rather than who does it. Swedish makes it by adding -s to the verb (s-passive) or with bli + participle. In speech, man is often used instead.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Huset byggdes för hundra år sedan. Mjölk säljs här. Han blev bjuden på fest.

rules.title: The s-passive
rules.explanation: Add -s to the active form. In the present, group 2 and 4 verbs drop -er before the -s (köper → köps). Group 1 present ends in -as.

examples.english: The shop opens (is opened) at nine.

examples.swedish: Huset byggdes för hundra år sedan.
examples.english: The house was built a hundred years ago.
examples.pronunciation: hewseht bewgdehs furr hewndrah ohr sehn.

examples.english: The book has been translated into Swedish.

rules.title: Who did it: av
rules.explanation: The doer (agent) is introduced with av.

examples.english: The meeting was led by the manager.

rules.title: bli + past participle and vara + past participle
rules.explanation: bli-passive stresses a change or a single event, and is common in speech. vara + participle describes a resulting state.

examples.english: He was invited to a party.

rules.title: s-passive after modals
rules.explanation: Very common in instructions and rules.

commonMistakes.why: For an event, use the s-passive (or bli); vara + participle describes a state.
Drop -er before -s in the present.

chapters.title: Deponent & Reciprocal -s Verbs
chapters.summary: Some verbs always end in -s but have an ACTIVE meaning (deponent verbs). Others use -s to mean 'each other' (reciprocal).
chapters.keyTakeaway: hoppas (hope), finnas (exist), trivas (enjoy/be happy somewhere); ses (see each other), träffas (meet).

rules.title: Deponent verbs
rules.explanation: These look passive but aren't. They have no form without -s.

rules.title: Reciprocal -s: each other
rules.explanation: -s on some verbs means the action goes both ways.

commonMistakes.wrong: Jag hoppar att du mår bra.
commonMistakes.right: Jag hoppas att du mår bra.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah hoppahs att dew mohr brah.
commonMistakes.why: hoppa = jump; hoppas = hope.

practice.prompt: Do you like it here? (feel at home)

chapters.title: Participles: stängd, skriven, sovande
chapters.summary: Past participles work like adjectives and agree with the noun (en/ett/plural). Present participles end in -ande/-ende and work like '-ing' adjectives or nouns.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Dörren är stängd, fönstret är stängt, dörrarna är stängda. en sovande katt.

rules.title: Past participle forms
rules.explanation: Formed from the verb group, then inflected like an adjective.

rules.title: Present participle: -ande / -ende
rules.explanation: -ande for most verbs, -ende for short verbs ending in a vowel other than -a (gå → gående). Used as adjective, noun, or with verbs of motion (kom springande).

commonMistakes.why: fönster is an ett-word, so the participle takes -t.
The -ande form isn't used for progressive tense.

chapters.title: Conditionals: om, skulle, vore
chapters.summary: Real conditions use om + present. Hypothetical conditions use om + past tense, with skulle + infinitive in the result. skulle is also the polite way to ask for things.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Om det regnar stannar vi hemma. Om jag hade pengar skulle jag resa. Skulle du kunna hjälpa mig?

rules.title: Real conditions
rules.explanation: om + present, then the main clause. When the om-clause comes first, the main clause inverts (verb before subject) — see 5.1.

examples.swedish: Om det regnar, stannar vi hemma.
examples.english: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
examples.pronunciation: omm deh rehgnahr, stannahr vee hehmmah.

examples.swedish: Vi stannar hemma om det regnar.
examples.english: We'll stay at home if it rains.
examples.pronunciation: vee stannahr hehmmah omm deh rehgnahr.

rules.title: Hypothetical present: om + past, skulle + infinitive
rules.explanation: vore is a formal past subjunctive of vara ('were'); var is fine in everyday speech.

examples.swedish: Om jag hade mer tid, skulle jag läsa mer.
examples.english: If I had more time, I would read more.
examples.pronunciation: omm yah hahdeh mehr teed, skewleh yah laisah mehr.

examples.swedish: Om jag vore du, skulle jag ringa henne.
examples.english: If I were you, I'd call her.
examples.pronunciation: omm yah vooreh dew, skewleh yah reengah hehnneh.

rules.title: Hypothetical past: om + hade, hade / skulle ha
rules.explanation: For things that didn't happen. hade can appear in both parts.

examples.swedish: Om jag hade vetat, hade jag kommit.
examples.english: If I had known, I would have come.
examples.pronunciation: omm yah hahdeh vehtaht, hahdeh yah kommeet.

examples.swedish: Jag skulle ha ringt om jag hade haft tid.
examples.english: I would have called if I had had time.
examples.pronunciation: yah skewleh hah reengt omm yah hahdeh hahft teed.

rules.title: Politeness with skulle
rules.explanation: skulle softens requests and wishes.

examples.swedish: Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe.
examples.pronunciation: yah skewleh vilyah hah ehn kaffeh.

commonMistakes.wrong: Om jag skulle ha pengar, skulle jag köpa en bil.
commonMistakes.right: Om jag hade pengar, skulle jag köpa en bil.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: omm yah hahdeh pehngahr, skewleh yah churpah ehn beel.
commonMistakes.english: If I had money, I would buy a car.
commonMistakes.why: The om-clause uses the past tense, not skulle.

commonMistakes.wrong: Om det regnar, vi stannar hemma.
commonMistakes.right: Om det regnar, stannar vi hemma.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: omm deh rehgnahr, stannahr vee hehmmah.
commonMistakes.english: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
commonMistakes.why: After a fronted om-clause, the verb comes before the subject.

practice.prompt: Om jag ___ (vara) rik, skulle jag resa jorden runt.
I would like to pay, please.
jag / om / tid / har / kommer / jag
practice.answer: Om jag har tid kommer jag.
acceptedAnswers: Om jag har tid kommer jag.

chapters.title: Infinitives With and Without att
chapters.summary: att is the infinitive marker ('to'). It is NOT used after modal verbs and a few others, but IS used after most other verbs, adjectives and prepositions.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag kan simma (no att). Jag gillar att simma (att). Jag är trött på att vänta (att after a preposition).

rules.title: No att after these
rules.explanation: Modals (kan, vill, ska, måste, får, bör), brukar, behöver, and verbs of perception with an object (se, höra).

rules.title: att after most other verbs
rules.explanation: With some verbs (börja, sluta, försöka, slippa) att is optional, and is often dropped in speech.

examples.swedish: Jag har glömt att låsa dörren.
examples.english: I forgot to lock the door.
examples.pronunciation: yah hahr glurmt att lohsah durrehn.

rules.title: Preposition + att + infinitive
rules.explanation: Where English uses a preposition + '-ing', Swedish uses preposition + att + infinitive.

examples.swedish: Jag är trött på att vänta.
examples.pronunciation: yah air trutt poh att ventah.

examples.swedish: Hon är bra på att sjunga.
examples.pronunciation: hoon air brah poh att shungah.

rules.title: för att = in order to; att as a noun
rules.explanation: för att + infinitive expresses purpose. An att-phrase can also be the subject.

examples.swedish: Jag flyttade hit för att studera.
examples.pronunciation: yah flewttahdeh heet furr att stewdehrah.

examples.swedish: Att lära sig svenska tar tid.
examples.pronunciation: att lairah say svehnskah tahr teed.

commonMistakes.right: Jag är bra på att sjunga.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah air brah poh att shungah.
commonMistakes.why: Preposition + verb needs att.
No att after modals.

practice.answer: Tack för att du hjälpte mig!
acceptedAnswers: Tack för att du hjälpte mig!

practice.prompt: I'm saving money to buy a car.
practice.answer: Jag sparar pengar för att köpa en bil.
acceptedAnswers: Jag sparar pengar för att köpa en bil.

chapters.title: Expressing '-ing': Ongoing Actions
chapters.summary: Swedish has no '-ing' tense. The plain present usually covers it, but to stress that something is in progress Swedes use 'hålla på att' or a position verb + och (sitter och läser).
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag håller på att laga mat. Hon sitter och läser. Han står och väntar.

rules.title: Plain present (default)
rules.explanation: Most of the time, the simple present is enough.

examples.swedish: Vad gör du? – Jag tittar på tv.
examples.english: What are you doing? – I'm watching TV.
examples.pronunciation: vahd yurr dew? – yah tittahr poh tehveh.

rules.title: hålla på att / med
rules.explanation: hålla på att + infinitive or hålla på med + noun stresses that something is in progress right now.

examples.swedish: Jag håller på att laga mat.
examples.pronunciation: yah hollehr poh att lahgah maht.

examples.swedish: Vi håller på med ett projekt.
examples.pronunciation: vee hollehr poh mehd ehtt prooyehkt.

rules.title: Position verb + och + verb
rules.explanation: sitta / stå / ligga + och + same tense describes what someone is doing in that position. Very natural Swedish.

examples.swedish: Han stod och väntade på bussen.
examples.english: He was (standing) waiting for the bus.
examples.pronunciation: hahn stood ock ventahdeh poh bussehn.

commonMistakes.right: Jag läser. / Jag sitter och läser.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah laisehr. / yah sittehr ock laisehr.
commonMistakes.why: -ande is never used as a progressive tense.
Both verbs must be in the same tense.

practice.prompt: I'm in the middle of moving.

parts.title: Part 5: Word Order & Sentence Building
parts.subtitle: The V2 rule, questions, where inte goes, subordinate clauses (the BIFF rule), relative clauses, indirect questions and emphasis. This is where Swedish sounds most different from English.

chapters.title: The V2 Rule: The Verb Is Always Second
chapters.summary: In a Swedish main clause, the finite verb (the one with tense) must be the SECOND element. If anything other than the subject comes first — a time word, a place, an object, a whole subordinate clause — the subject moves after the verb.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag dricker kaffe i dag → I dag dricker jag kaffe. (Never 'I dag jag dricker'.)

rules.title: The main-clause template
rules.explanation: Position 1 (the 'fundament') can be almost anything, but position 2 is always the finite verb.

examples.swedish: I Stockholm finns det många museer.
examples.english: In Stockholm there are many museums.
examples.pronunciation: ee stockholm finns deh mohngah mewsehehr.

examples.swedish: Den filmen har jag redan sett.
examples.pronunciation: dehn feelmehn hahr yah rehdahn sehtt.

rules.title: A fronted subordinate clause counts as position 1
rules.explanation: When a sentence starts with a när-, om-, eftersom-clause etc., the main clause starts with its verb.

examples.swedish: När jag kom hem, åt jag middag.
examples.english: When I got home, I had dinner.
examples.pronunciation: nair yah komm hehm, oht yah middahg.

examples.swedish: Eftersom det var kallt, tog jag en jacka.
examples.english: Since it was cold, I took a jacket.
examples.pronunciation: ehftehrsomm deh vahr kallt, toog yah ehn yackah.

rules.title: Words that DON'T take up position 1
rules.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions (och, men, eller, för, så) and interjections (ja, nej, jo) sit outside the template and don't trigger inversion.

examples.swedish: Jag är trött, men jag går ut.
examples.english: I'm tired, but I'm going out.
examples.pronunciation: yah air trutt, mehn yah gohr ewt.

commonMistakes.why: The verb must be second.
sedan (then) takes position 1, so the verb follows.

practice.prompt: på morgonen / jag / kaffe / dricker (start with 'På morgonen')
I morgon vi åker till Uppsala.
practice.answer: I morgon åker vi till Uppsala.
acceptedAnswers: I morgon åker vi till Uppsala.

chapters.title: Asking Questions
chapters.summary: Yes/no questions start with the verb. Question-word questions put the question word first, then the verb, then the subject. No 'do/does' is needed.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Talar du svenska? Var bor du? Vem kommer?

rules.title: Yes/no questions: verb first
rules.explanation: Swap subject and verb.

rules.title: Question words + verb + subject
rules.explanation: vad, vem, var, vart, när, varför, hur, vilken/vilket/vilka. Note var (where, location) vs vart (where to, direction).

examples.swedish: Hur länge har du bott här?
examples.english: How long have you lived here?
examples.pronunciation: hewr lengeh hahr dew bott hair?

rules.title: When the question word is the subject
rules.explanation: If vem or vad IS the subject, it is followed directly by the verb.

rules.title: Tag questions
rules.explanation: eller hur? (right?) and va? (informal) turn a statement into a question.

commonMistakes.why: Yes/no questions start with the verb (statement order only works as surprised intonation).
Question word + verb + subject.

chapters.title: Negation & Sentence Adverbs in Main Clauses
chapters.summary: inte and other sentence adverbs (aldrig, alltid, ofta, också, redan, kanske, bara, gärna, nog) go directly AFTER the finite verb — or after the subject if the subject comes after the verb.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag dricker inte kaffe. I dag dricker jag inte kaffe. Jag har inte druckit kaffe.

rules.title: Basic position
rules.explanation: verb + inte in straight order; verb + subject + inte in inverted order and questions.

examples.english: Maybe we'll see each other tomorrow.

rules.title: Unstressed pronoun objects move before inte (B2)
rules.explanation: In simple tenses, short object pronouns (mig, dig, honom, det, den...) jump in front of inte. With auxiliaries (har, ska, kan) they don't.

examples.swedish: Jag vet inte. / Det vet jag inte.
examples.pronunciation: yah veht eenteh. / deh veht yah eenteh.

rules.title: också, inte heller
rules.explanation: också = also/too; inte heller = not ... either.

commonMistakes.why: inte follows the finite verb in a main clause.
V2 first, then subject, then inte.
inte goes after har, before the supine.

practice.prompt: Make it negative: Jag talar tyska.
Make it negative: I kväll ska vi gå ut.
practice.answer: I kväll ska vi inte gå ut.
acceptedAnswers: I kväll ska vi inte gå ut.

practice.prompt: har / aldrig / jag / i Kiruna / varit
practice.answer: Jag har aldrig varit i Kiruna.
acceptedAnswers: Jag har aldrig varit i Kiruna.

chapters.title: Subordinate Clauses & the BIFF Rule
chapters.summary: In subordinate clauses (after att, om, när, eftersom, som...) there is NO inversion, and inte and other sentence adverbs come BEFORE the finite verb. Swedes remember it as BIFF: Bisats – Inte – Före – Finita verbet.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Main: Han kommer inte. Subordinate: ...att han inte kommer.

rules.title: The subordinate-clause template
rules.explanation: Subjunction → subject → sentence adverb → finite verb → rest.

examples.swedish: Jag vet att han inte kommer.
examples.english: I know that he isn't coming.
examples.pronunciation: yah veht att hahn eenteh kommehr.

examples.swedish: Hon säger att hon alltid läser på kvällen.
examples.english: She says that she always reads in the evening.
examples.pronunciation: hoon saiyehr att hoon allteed laisehr poh kvellehn.

examples.swedish: Ring mig om du inte hittar.
examples.english: Call me if you can't find the way.
examples.pronunciation: reeng may omm dew eenteh hittahr.

rules.title: Common subjunctions
rules.explanation: These introduce subordinate clauses.

examples.swedish: Jag stannar hemma eftersom jag inte mår bra.
examples.english: I'm staying home because I'm not feeling well.
examples.pronunciation: yah stannahr hehmmah ehftehrsomm yah eenteh mohr brah.

rules.title: att can be dropped
rules.explanation: In speech, att is often dropped after verbs like säga, tro, tycka, veta — but the subordinate word order stays.

commonMistakes.wrong: Jag vet att han kommer inte.
commonMistakes.right: Jag vet att han inte kommer.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah veht att hahn eenteh kommehr.
commonMistakes.why: BIFF: in a subordinate clause, inte goes before the finite verb.
No inversion inside a subordinate clause.

practice.prompt: Combine: Hon säger något. Hon har inte tid. → Hon säger att ___
practice.answer: Hon säger att hon inte har tid.
acceptedAnswers: Hon säger att hon inte har tid.

practice.prompt: Jag är glad eftersom jag har inte jobbat i dag.
practice.answer: Jag är glad eftersom jag inte har jobbat i dag.
acceptedAnswers: Jag är glad eftersom jag inte har jobbat i dag.

practice.prompt: om / du / kan / jag / undrar / komma
practice.answer: Jag undrar om du kan komma.
acceptedAnswers: Jag undrar om du kan komma.

chapters.title: Coordinating Conjunctions: och, men, eller, för, så
chapters.summary: Coordinating conjunctions join two main clauses, so both clauses keep normal main-clause word order. Watch the difference between för (because + main clause) and eftersom (because + subordinate clause).
chapters.keyTakeaway: ...för jag är inte hungrig. vs ...eftersom jag inte är hungrig.

rules.title: Main clause after och, men, eller, för, så
rules.explanation: inte comes after the verb, just like any main clause.

examples.swedish: Jag äter inte, för jag är inte hungrig.
examples.english: I'm not eating because I'm not hungry.
examples.pronunciation: yah aitehr eenteh, furr yah air eenteh hungree.

examples.swedish: Det regnade, så vi stannade inne.
examples.english: It was raining, so we stayed inside.
examples.pronunciation: deh rehgnahdeh, soh vee stannahdeh inneh.

rules.title: för vs eftersom
rules.explanation: Same meaning, different word order. eftersom-clauses can also come first; för-clauses can't.

examples.swedish: Jag går hem, för jag är trött.
examples.english: I'm going home because I'm tired.
examples.pronunciation: yah gohr hehm, furr yah air trutt.

examples.swedish: Eftersom jag är trött, går jag hem.
examples.english: Since I'm tired, I'm going home.
examples.pronunciation: ehftehrsomm yah air trutt, gohr yah hehm.

rules.title: så (so) vs så (then)
rules.explanation: As 'so/therefore' så is a conjunction (no inversion). As 'then', it is an adverb in position 1 and triggers inversion.

examples.swedish: Jag var sjuk, så jag stannade hemma.
examples.english: I was ill, so I stayed at home.
examples.pronunciation: yah vahr shewk, soh yah stannahdeh hehmmah.

examples.swedish: Först åt vi, så gick vi ut.
examples.english: First we ate, then we went out.
examples.pronunciation: furrst oht vee, soh yick vee ewt.

commonMistakes.why: för is followed by a main clause.

practice.prompt: Jag tar bussen, ___ jag har ingen bil.
practice.explanation: 'jag har ingen bil' has main-clause order; with eftersom it would be 'eftersom jag inte har någon bil'.

practice.answer: Hon är trött, men hon är glad.
acceptedAnswers: Hon är trött, men hon är glad.

chapters.title: Relative Clauses: som, där, vars, vilket
chapters.summary: som means 'who / which / that' for both people and things. It can be left out when it isn't the subject. There are also där (where), vars (whose) and vilket (which, about a whole idea).
chapters.keyTakeaway: Mannen som bor här. Boken (som) jag läser. Staden där jag bor.

rules.title: som for people and things
rules.explanation: som can be dropped only when it is the object of the relative clause.

examples.swedish: Mannen som bor här är läkare.
examples.english: The man who lives here is a doctor.
examples.pronunciation: mahnnehn soom boor hair air laikahreh.

examples.english: The book (that) I'm reading is exciting.

rules.title: BIFF applies here too
rules.explanation: Relative clauses are subordinate clauses, so inte goes before the verb.

examples.swedish: Det är en film som jag inte har sett.
examples.english: It's a film I haven't seen.
examples.pronunciation: deh air ehn feelm soom yah eenteh hahr sehtt.

rules.title: Preposition at the end
rules.explanation: Swedish puts the preposition at the end of the relative clause.

examples.swedish: Huset (som) jag bor i är gammalt.
examples.english: The house I live in is old.
examples.pronunciation: hewseht (soom) yah boor ee air gammahlt.

examples.swedish: Hon är den (som) jag pratade med.
examples.english: She's the one I talked to.
examples.pronunciation: hoon air dehn (soom) yah prahtahdeh mehd.

rules.title: där, vars, vilket
rules.explanation: där = where (place); vars = whose; vilket = which, referring to a whole statement.

examples.swedish: Staden där jag bor heter Västerås.
examples.english: The town where I live is called Västerås.
examples.pronunciation: stahdehn dair yah boor hehtehr vestehrohs.

examples.swedish: Kvinnan vars bil blev stulen ringde polisen.
examples.english: The woman whose car was stolen called the police.
examples.pronunciation: kvinnahn vahrs beel blehv stewlehn reengdeh pooleesehn.

examples.swedish: Han kom inte, vilket var konstigt.
examples.english: He didn't come, which was strange.
examples.pronunciation: hahn komm eenteh, vilkeht vahr konstee.

commonMistakes.right: Mannen som bor här är läkare.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: mahnnehn soom boor hair air laikahreh.
commonMistakes.english: The man who lives here is a doctor.
commonMistakes.why: som can't be dropped when it's the subject.

commonMistakes.wrong: Huset i vilket jag bor... (in speech)
commonMistakes.why: Correct but stiff; everyday Swedish puts the preposition last.

practice.prompt: Det är kvinnan ___ jag träffade i går.
The restaurant where we ate was good.
practice.answer: Restaurangen där vi åt var bra.
acceptedAnswers: Restaurangen där vi åt var bra.

practice.prompt: That's the friend I told you about.
practice.answer: Det är vännen (som) jag berättade om.
acceptedAnswers: Det är vännen som jag berättade om.
Det är vännen jag berättade om.

chapters.title: Indirect Questions & Reported Speech
chapters.summary: When a question is embedded in a sentence ('I wonder where he lives'), it becomes a subordinate clause: question word or om (whether) + subject + verb. When the question word is the subject, add som.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Var bor han? → Jag undrar var han bor. Vem kommer? → Jag vet inte vem som kommer.

rules.title: Question word + straight word order
rules.explanation: No inversion, and BIFF applies.

examples.english: Do you know where the station is?
He asked what my name was.

rules.title: Yes/no questions become om
rules.explanation: om = whether / if.

examples.swedish: Jag undrar om du kan hjälpa mig.
examples.english: I wonder if you can help me.
examples.pronunciation: yah ewndrahr omm dew kahn yelpah may.

examples.swedish: Hon frågade om jag inte var hungrig.
examples.english: She asked if I wasn't hungry.
examples.pronunciation: hoon frohgahdeh omm yah eenteh vahr hungree.

rules.title: vem som, vad som, vilka som
rules.explanation: When the question word is the subject of the embedded clause, add som.

examples.swedish: Jag vet inte vem som ringde.
examples.pronunciation: yah veht eenteh vemm soom reengdeh.

rules.title: Reported speech and tense
rules.explanation: After a reporting verb in the past (sa, frågade), the reported verb usually moves to the past too.

examples.swedish: ”Jag är trött.” → Hon sa att hon var trött.
examples.english: 'I'm tired.' → She said she was tired.
examples.pronunciation: yah air trutt. → hoon sah att hoon vahr trutt.

commonMistakes.english: Do you know where the station is?
commonMistakes.why: Embedded questions use straight word order.

commonMistakes.right: Jag vet inte vem som ringde.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah veht eenteh vemm soom reengdeh.
commonMistakes.why: Add som when the question word is the subject.

practice.prompt: Make it indirect: När börjar filmen? → Vet du ___
Make it indirect: Kommer hon? → Jag undrar ___
Make it indirect: Vad hände? → Ingen vet ___

chapters.title: Emphasis: Fronting and 'Det är ... som'
chapters.summary: Swedish shifts focus by moving things to position 1, or by using a cleft sentence: Det är/var X som... Clefts are extremely common in Swedish questions.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Det var Anna som ringde. Vem var det som ringde? Vad är det som händer?

rules.title: Cleft sentences
rules.explanation: Det är / det var + the focused part + som (or nothing, if not the subject) + rest.

examples.swedish: Det är i morgon vi åker.
examples.pronunciation: deh air ee morron vee ohkehr.

rules.title: Clefts in questions
rules.explanation: These sound natural and slightly softer than plain questions.

examples.swedish: Var det du som lagade maten?
examples.english: Was it you who cooked the food?
examples.pronunciation: vahr deh dew soom lahgahdeh mahtehn?

rules.title: Fronting for contrast
rules.explanation: Put the contrasted element first; the verb still comes second.

examples.swedish: Kaffe dricker jag inte, men te älskar jag.
examples.english: Coffee I don't drink, but tea I love.
examples.pronunciation: kaffeh drickehr yah eenteh, mehn teh elskahr yah.

commonMistakes.why: som is required when the focused part is the subject.

practice.prompt: It was my brother who paid.
practice.answer: Det var min bror som betalade.
acceptedAnswers: Det var min bror som betalade.

practice.prompt: What is it that you want?
acceptedAnswers: Vad är det som du vill?

parts.title: Part 6: Prepositions, Time & Small Words
parts.subtitle: i vs på, time expressions, movement vs location, the lie/lay and sit/set verb pairs, numbers and dates, and the little words (ju, väl, nog, jo) that make Swedish sound natural.

chapters.title: i vs på (Place)
chapters.summary: i is for being inside something enclosed, and for cities and countries. på is for surfaces, islands, and many workplaces, institutions and events. Some combinations simply have to be learned.
chapters.keyTakeaway: i Sverige, i köket, i bilen — på bordet, på jobbet, på Gotland, på bio.

rules.title: When to use i
rules.explanation: Inside a space, a container or a vehicle; cities, countries, regions; rooms.

examples.english: The keys are in the bag.

rules.title: When to use på
rules.explanation: On surfaces; on islands; and at most workplaces, public places and events.

examples.english: The book is on the table.
Shall we go to the cinema?

rows: på bordet, på väggen, på golvet
på Gotland, på Öland, på Kreta
på jobbet, på kontoret, på banken, på sjukhuset, på universitetet
på bio, på restaurang, på fest, på konsert, på semester

rules.title: Exceptions to memorise
rules.explanation: Some places take i even though English says 'at'.

rules.title: Other place prepositions
rules.explanation: vid (by/at), hos (at someone's place), bredvid (next to), mellan (between), framför (in front of), bakom (behind), under, över.

examples.english: The car is in front of the house.

commonMistakes.why: Workplaces take på.
Cities take i.

chapters.title: Time Expressions & Prepositions
chapters.summary: Swedish time prepositions change with past, present and future: i (duration / this), för ... sedan (ago), om (in, future), på (within / negative duration).
chapters.keyTakeaway: i två år (for two years), för två år sedan (two years ago), om två år (in two years), på två år (in/within two years; not for two years).

rules.title: Duration and point in time
rules.explanation: These four are the most important time prepositions.

examples.swedish: Jag har bott här i tre år.
examples.english: I've lived here for three years.
examples.pronunciation: yah hahr bott hair ee treh ohr.

examples.swedish: Hon kom hit för en månad sedan.
examples.english: She came here a month ago.
examples.pronunciation: hoon komm heet furr ehn mohnahd sehn.

examples.english: The bus leaves in five minutes.

examples.swedish: Vi har inte setts på länge!
examples.english: We haven't seen each other for ages!
examples.pronunciation: vee hahr eenteh sehtts poh lengeh!

rows: Jag har bott här i tre år.
Jag flyttade hit för tre år sedan.
within / in (+ not for, in negatives)
Jag gjorde det på en timme. / Jag har inte sett honom på länge.

rules.title: Days, parts of the day and seasons: this / last / next
rules.explanation: Swedish uses special forms: i + -s for 'last', på for 'next', i for 'this'.

examples.english: What did you do last summer?

rules.title: Habits: på + definite form
rules.explanation: For repeated times, use på + the definite form (or på + plural -ar-na for weekdays).

examples.english: In the mornings I drink coffee.

commonMistakes.wrong: Jag har bott här för tre år.
commonMistakes.right: Jag har bott här i tre år.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah hahr bott hair ee treh ohr.
commonMistakes.english: I've lived here for three years.
commonMistakes.why: Duration uses i, not för.
på måndag means NEXT Monday.

practice.prompt: I started learning Swedish two months ago.
practice.answer: Jag började lära mig svenska för två månader sedan.
acceptedAnswers: Jag började lära mig svenska för två månader sedan.

practice.prompt: What are you doing this weekend?

chapters.title: Movement vs Location: hem/hemma, ut/ute...
chapters.summary: Swedish uses different adverbs for going somewhere (movement) and being somewhere (location). The short form is for movement, the longer form for location.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Jag går hem (movement). Jag är hemma (location).

rules.title: The pairs
rules.explanation: Ask yourself: is something moving there, or is it already there?

commonMistakes.why: Movement towards = hit.
Location = hemma.
Direction = vart.

chapters.title: Position Verb Pairs: ligga/lägga, sitta/sätta, stå/ställa
chapters.summary: Swedish distinguishes between BEING in a position (ligga, sitta, stå) and PUTTING something in a position (lägga, sätta, ställa). Swedes also use these verbs where English just says 'is'.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Boken ligger på bordet. Jag lägger boken på bordet.

rules.title: The three pairs
rules.explanation: The 'putting' verbs need an object (or a reflexive: lägga sig, sätta sig, ställa sig).

examples.english: I put the keys on the table.
The keys are on the table.
Put the bottle in the fridge.
The bottle is in the fridge.

rules.title: Where English just says 'is'
rules.explanation: Swedes often describe where things are with the position verb.

examples.english: The painting is on the wall.
It says so in the newspaper.

commonMistakes.english: I put the book on the table.
commonMistakes.why: Putting something = lägga.
The action of sitting down is sätta sig.

chapters.title: Numbers, Ordinals, Dates & Telling Time
chapters.summary: Builds on the numbers in the vocabulary book: teens, tens, ordinals (första, andra...), how to say dates and years, and the Swedish way of telling time with 'halv' and 'i'/'över'.
chapters.keyTakeaway: den tjugoandra oktober; halv tre = 2:30 (half TO three); fem över halv tre = 2:35.

rules.title: Numbers 13–1000
rules.explanation: Compound numbers are written as one word: tjugofem (25), hundrafemtio (150).

rules.title: Ordinal numbers
rules.explanation: Used for dates, floors and order.

examples.english: I live on the third floor.

rules.title: Dates and years
rules.explanation: Say 'den' + ordinal + month. Months and weekdays are lowercase. Years: 2026 = tjugohundratjugosex or tvåtusentjugosex; 1995 = nittonhundranittiofem.

examples.swedish: I dag är det den tjugoandra oktober.
examples.pronunciation: ee dah air deh dehn chewgooahndrah oktoobehr.

rules.title: Telling the time
rules.explanation: halv = half TO the next hour. 'i' = to, 'över' = past. Minutes near half past are counted from halv. Written times use 24h with a dot: 14.30.

examples.swedish: Vad är klockan? – Den är halv fyra.
examples.english: What time is it? – It's half past three.
examples.pronunciation: vahd air klockahn? – dehn air hahlv fewrah.

examples.english: See you at quarter past seven.

commonMistakes.why: halv means halfway TO the next hour.
Months are lowercase.

practice.prompt: Write in words: the 1st of May → den ___ maj

chapters.title: Ja, Jo, Nej & Little Words: ju, väl, nog
chapters.summary: Swedish has a special 'yes' (jo) for contradicting a negative question, plus small unstressed words (ju, väl, nog, visst) that add attitude and make speech sound natural.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Kommer du inte? – Jo! (Yes, I am!). Det är ju fredag! (It's Friday, you know!)

rules.title: ja vs jo
rules.explanation: Answer a negative question with jo when you mean 'yes'. Answering ja would sound like you agree with the negative.

examples.english: Aren't you coming? – Yes, of course I am!

examples.swedish: Har du inte ätit? – Nej, inte än.
examples.english: Haven't you eaten? – No, not yet.
examples.pronunciation: hahr dew eenteh aiteet? – nay, eenteh ehn.

rules.title: Modal particles
rules.explanation: These are unstressed and placed like sentence adverbs (after the finite verb).

rules.title: Feedback words in conversation
rules.explanation: Swedes signal listening with short sounds and words: mm, precis (exactly), just det (that's right), jaså (oh really?), oj (oops/wow), aha.

commonMistakes.wrong: Gillar du inte kaffe? – Ja, jag älskar det!
commonMistakes.right: Gillar du inte kaffe? – Jo, jag älskar det!
commonMistakes.english: Don't you like coffee? – Yes, I love it!
commonMistakes.why: Contradicting a negative question needs jo.

practice.prompt: Har du inte varit i Sverige? – ___, två gånger!

parts.title: Part 7: Polishing Your Swedish (B1–B2)
parts.subtitle: Spoken vs written forms, building words with prefixes and suffixes, easily confused verbs, and a final checklist of the most common learner errors.

chapters.title: Spoken vs Written Swedish
chapters.summary: Many words are written one way and said another. Knowing both helps you understand native speakers and write correctly.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Write 'de', 'dem', 'mig', 'sedan' — say 'dom', 'dom', 'mej', 'sen'.

rules.title: Common written ↔ spoken pairs
rules.explanation: In texts and chat messages, the spoken forms are increasingly accepted informally.

examples.english: Have you got something to drink?

rules.title: Formal vs informal style
rules.explanation: Swedish is very informal: du is used with almost everyone, including bosses and strangers. ni as a polite singular 'you' is rare and can even sound distant. First names are the norm.

examples.swedish: Hej, vad kan jag hjälpa dig med?
examples.english: Hi, what can I help you with?
examples.pronunciation: hay, vahd kahn yah yelpah day mehd?

commonMistakes.wrong: Dom bor här. (in a formal text)
commonMistakes.why: dom is spoken; write de/dem in formal texts.

practice.prompt: Write in standard Swedish: Ja såg nån där.
Write in standard Swedish: Han sa att dom kommer sen.
practice.answer: Han sa att de kommer sedan.
acceptedAnswers: Han sa att de kommer sedan.

chapters.title: Word Formation: Prefixes & Suffixes
chapters.summary: Recognising common prefixes and suffixes lets you understand and build hundreds of new words from ones you already know.
chapters.keyTakeaway: o- = un- (olycklig); -het makes nouns (lycklig → lycklighet); -bar = -able (läsbar).

rules.title: Prefixes
rules.explanation: The prefix usually takes the stress.

rules.title: Suffixes
rules.explanation: Suffixes often decide gender too.

rows: snabb → snabbhet, fri → frihet, ny → nyhet

commonMistakes.why: The Swedish negative prefix is o-.

chapters.title: Easily Confused Words
chapters.summary: Several English verbs split into two or three Swedish verbs with different meanings. Choosing the right one is a big step towards sounding natural.
chapters.keyTakeaway: tycka (opinion), tro (believe), tänka (think in your head); veta (fact), känna (person), kunna (skill).

rules.title: think: tycka, tro, tänka
rules.explanation: tycka = have an opinion from experience; tro = believe, guess; tänka = think (the mental process) or plan to.

examples.swedish: Jag tycker att filmen är bra.
examples.english: I think the film is good. (opinion)
examples.pronunciation: yah tickehr att feelmehn air brah.

examples.swedish: Jag tror att det blir regn.
examples.pronunciation: yah troor att deh bleer rehgn.

rules.title: know: veta, känna, kunna
rules.explanation: veta = know a fact; känna = know a person (or känna till = know about); kunna = know a skill or language.

rules.title: go: gå, åka, köra, resa
rules.explanation: gå = walk / go on foot (also of trains and buses leaving); åka = travel by vehicle; köra = drive; resa = travel, take a trip.

examples.english: I take the bus to work.

rules.title: live: bo vs leva; learn: lära sig vs lära
rules.explanation: bo = live somewhere; leva = be alive / live a life. lära sig = learn; lära (ut) = teach; plugga = study (informal).

examples.english: She teaches the children to swim.

rules.title: The many meanings of få
rules.explanation: få = get/receive, may/be allowed to, and (in the past) had to.

examples.english: We had to wait an hour.

commonMistakes.why: People = känna.

commonMistakes.wrong: Jag tänker att det är bra.
commonMistakes.right: Jag tycker att det är bra.
commonMistakes.pronunciation: yah tickehr att deh air brah.
commonMistakes.why: Opinions = tycka.
Where you live = bo.

chapters.title: Final Checklist: The 12 Most Common Learner Errors
chapters.summary: Run through this list when you check your own writing. Each point links back to the chapter that explains it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Check: verb second, inte placement, en/ett agreement, sin vs hans, and no 'att' after modals.

rules.title: The checklist
rules.explanation: Most errors in Swedish texts by learners fall into these categories.

examples.swedish: I går såg jag en bra film som jag inte hade sett förut.
examples.english: Yesterday I saw a good film that I hadn't seen before.
examples.pronunciation: ee gohr soh yah ehn brah feelm soom yah eenteh hahdeh sehtt furrewt.
examples.note: Uses V2, past tense with a time word, and BIFF in the relative clause.

rows: I dag jag jobbar → I dag jobbar jag
inte after the verb in main clauses
Jag inte vet → Jag vet inte
inte before the verb in subordinate clauses
...att han kommer inte → ...att han inte kommer
ett stor hus → ett stort hus
den stora bil → den stora bilen
sin/sitt/sina for the subject's own things
Hon ringer hennes mamma → Hon ringer sin mamma
Jag kan att simma → Jag kan simma
Past tense with a specific past time
Jag har sett den i går → Jag såg den i går
för två år → i två år
